description_full: Canadian Natural Resources Limited engages in the acquisition, exploration, development, production, marketing, and sale of crude oil, natural gas, and natural gas liquids (NGLs) in Western Canada, the United Kingdom sector of the North Sea, and Offshore Africa. The company offers synthetic crude oil (SCO), mining bitumen, light and medium crude oil and NGLs, thermal bitumen, primary heavy crude oil and Pelican Lake heavy crude oil. Its midstream assets include two crude oil pipeline systems; and a 50% working interest in an 84-megawatt cogeneration plant at Primrose. The company was formerly known as AEX Minerals Corporation and changed its name to Canadian Natural Resources Limited in December 1975. Canadian Natural Resources Limited was incorporated in 1973 and is headquartered in Calgary, Canada.

financial_summary: Canadian Natural Resources Limi is a large-cap energy business with a $100.1B market cap on $27.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -5% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 8% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 14× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.2% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 3.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.

sect: Its 37% operating margin runs 21pp above the Energy median (16%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 57% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 14% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.61, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.88 vs 5y 0.46), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $314.5M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 76% in the 2020 crash, 32% in the 2022 bear market and 75% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 16% below its blended-model fair value of $57.54, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 0%).
On multiples it looks cheap against Energy peers: P/E 9.9 vs 13.4 and EV/EBITDA 5.3 vs 6.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 68% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an EBIT/EV of 9.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $48.89 on average, 1% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.61).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.40x.
ROE of 24% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 11pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.7x net debt to EBITDA ($476.4M of cash against $11.4B of debt), with interest covered 13.7x.
The current ratio of 0.95 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -5.2% over 3 years and 17.1% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 34%).
own: Insiders own a modest 2.2%, and institutions hold 79%.
It returns 4.5% a year to shareholders (1.0% in buybacks and 3.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 25 consecutive years, raising it 19.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 10,750 employees, each generates about $2.6M of revenue, 1.3x the Energy median, and productivity has risen 10.1% a year.
CEO pay is $10.2M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
